newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Rule of law showcased as Hanoi drugs trial begins.
newsitem.headline: Rule of law showcased as Hanoi drugs trial begins.

text.p: A major narcotics trial opened in Vietnam on Friday, casting the spotlight on police corruption and the government's determination to bolster the rule of law.
Hundreds of people, including several tearful relatives of the accused, gathered at Hanoi People's Court as a convoy of police jeeps and trucks carrying the 22 defendants pulled up outside.

Among the accused were 11 police officers and border guards. One, a drugs-squad captain, vowed earlier this week to expose some "extremely important people" during the hearing in exchange for an amnesty from execution for two relatives also on trial.

Vietnam's official media carried extensive details of the case on Friday, including prison interviews with key defendants -- one of whom tried to commit suicide while in jail. Top government officials were quoted as saying nothing would be allowed to stand in the way of justice.

"The process (of law) will be continued and will not be stopped," said Interior Ministry Le Minh Huong in an interview with the Lao Dong newspaper. "(The government) is determined not to let the case sink. Don't worry."
The scandal dates back to January 1995 when two Laotian nationals were arrested in Vietnam after they were found in posession of 15 kg (33 pounds) of heroin.
One of the men, Sieng Pheng, earned a last-minute reprieve from execution after breaking down in front of a firing squad and offering information which later led to the arrest of around 30 people.
Pheng said heroin concealed in his car was just part of his delivery and that more had been hidden in a false bottom of the car's fuel tank.
Five police officers were charged with stealing the drugs after a subsequent examination of the fuel tank found it empty.

The trial comes at a time of rising concern in Vietnam that the impoverished communist country is becoming a conduit and market for drugs from Asia's notorious Golden Triangle which straddles the borders of Laos, China, Thailand and Burma.

But it also follows in the wake of a series of high-profile trials showcasing top-level determination to crack down on social vices, including corruption, which are seen as having flourished in the wake of reform policies launched in the late 1980s.
In recent months a number of people, including Communist Party officials, have been sentenced to death on corruption charges, in most cases associated with business activities.

Vietnam's police authorities are responsible for internal security and hold huge power in the communist establishment. But the presiding judge was quoted on Friday as saying the rule of law would be fearless, coming above power and influence.
"We are really worried, because if the result is not satisfactory then our reputation among the people will be affected," Dang Minh Ngoc told the Lao Dong newspaper.
"The board of judges will issue orders to march (key witnesses) to court if they refuse to appear, despite who they are, what they are doing and which position they are occupying."
The trial is expected to last around 10 days. Ngoc said earlier that 10 of the defendants were likely to face the death penalty.
